comparison: Both evaluations address the computational modeling claims (C47-C48). OpenEval finds the model predictions agree well with experimental observations. Peer reviewers accept the modeling as valid but note it's not necessary since the predictions are intuitive to those familiar with Notch signaling.

Both evaluations address the JNK/Pak molecular pathway claims (C56-C63). OpenEval finds comprehensive support through genetic interactions, reporter assays, and biochemical measurements. Peer reviewers do not raise concerns about this pathway data, accepting it as part of the globally well-supported findings.

Both address temporal requirement claims (C64-C65). OpenEval finds the critical period well-established through temperature-sensitive allele experiments. Peer reviewers accept this data without challenge as part of the well-supported findings.

Both address gain-of-function claims (C66-C67). OpenEval finds bidirectional effects strengthen the conclusion about Notch activity regulating target choice. Peer reviewers accept this data without raising concerns.

Both address compensation mechanism claims (C72-C73, with C5 also in peer review). OpenEval finds strong evidence for compensation by neighboring cells. However, peer reviewers raise a specific concern about Figure 8i showing a cluster of one mutant and one wild-type axon, which appears counter to the compensation model.

Both address quantitative characterization of DCN variability and stereotypy (C24-C32 overlap). OpenEval finds comprehensive support with appropriate statistical analyses. Peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge 'very careful quantification' and accept the paradox of variable cell numbers producing stereotyped connectivity.

Both address 3D positional analysis and subcluster competition (C38-C42). OpenEval finds strong quantitative support for local interactions. Peer reviewers accept this data as part of the careful quantification without raising concerns.

Both address dissociation between positional information and target choice (C33-C34, C36-C37). OpenEval finds strong statistical support ruling out simple positional determinism. Peer reviewers accept this as part of the quantification data showing variability in projections despite stereotypy.

Both address where Notch functions (C79). OpenEval finds the inference about cell body interactions reasonably supported by Su(H)/Mam requirements and E(spl) reporter data, though acknowledges axonal interactions cannot be formally excluded. Peer reviewers explicitly request clarification on whether Delta/Notch signaling functions in axons or soma, indicating uncertainty about this claim.

Both address core mechanism claims (C2-C6). OpenEval finds converging experimental evidence from genetic manipulations and clone analyses establishing Notch-mediated mutual inhibition. Peer reviewers state this is 'an interesting finding, which is globally well supported by the data' and acknowledge the surprising re-utilization of lateral inhibition in postmitotic neurons.

Both address fate marker claims (C54-C55). OpenEval finds controls showing no effect on fate markers support the conclusion. However, peer reviewers raise a major concern that only two molecular markers (Acj6 and Ato) are shown to be identical, questioning whether this sufficiently demonstrates that Notch choice is independent of cell fate, suggesting the two populations might actually be different cell types.

Both address genetic validation of Notch pathway (C49-C53). OpenEval finds comprehensive support with multiple pathway components tested and appropriate controls. Peer reviewers accept this as part of the globally well-supported evidence for lateral inhibition mechanism.

Both address Notch signaling components and heterogeneity (C43-C46). OpenEval finds support through immunohistochemistry and reporter gene expression. Peer reviewers accept this as part of the evidence supporting the lateral inhibition mechanism without raising concerns.

Both address cell autonomy claims (C68-C71). OpenEval finds strong support through MARCM single-cell analysis with appropriate statistical testing. Peer reviewers accept this as part of the globally well-supported findings for the lateral inhibition mechanism.

Both address multi-cell clone compensation failure (C75-C77). OpenEval finds strong support through novel genetic approach creating adjacent mutant clones. Peer reviewers accept this as part of the evidence supporting the mutual inhibition model without raising specific concerns.

Both address novelty and model synthesis claims (C78, C80). OpenEval finds the novelty claim justified by postmitotic timing and probabilistic nature. Peer reviewers acknowledge this is 'surprising' and represents a re-utilization of lateral inhibition pathway, accepting the overall model.

OpenEval addresses conceptual and evolutionary arguments (C7-C9, C82-C83) and finds them logical but speculative without direct experimental support. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these broader conceptual claims.

OpenEval addresses background and prior work claims (C10-C22), finding they accurately summarize established knowledge with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found as reviewers typically do not evaluate literature review sections.

Peer reviewers raise major concern about whether Notch choice is truly independent of cell fate (C3, C27, C54-C55), questioning if only two molecular markers are sufficient and whether the populations might actually be different cell types with Notch functioning classically in fate determination. While OpenEval addresses some of these claims in R1 and R7 with SUPPORTED status, the peer review groups them distinctly as a major unresolved question about the fundamental interpretation.
